items.summary: Supplementary material and reproducibility package for the article Probing Coherent Noise with Stabilizer Codes: Identifiability, Ambiguity, and Decoder Priors . The supplement analyses the null result of a recent repetition-code experiment (arXiv:2606.07377), in which the logical fidelity of d = 3 and d = 5 bit-flip repetition codes was found to be indistinguishable under coherent and stochastic error injection, contrary to the circuit-level simulation of that work. It establishes three results, each independently checkable: The average gate infidelity of a coherent rotation is exactly invariant under randomization of its rotation axis by a drifting frame phase, so no fidelity-based comparison can detect such randomization at all. For a bit-flip repetition code read out in the computational basis, an X-type coherent injection and a stochastic injection of equal single-site average fidelity give logical error probabilities that agree to machine precision (3×10 −15 ), for d = 3 and d = 5, R = 10 rounds, with and without syndrome misreports. items.summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and its corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond selecting the number of inference steps and achieves substantially shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.
items.title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Flow for Inverse Problems

items.summary: Flow matching models have emerged as a dominant paradigm for generative posterior sampling in imaging inverse problems. Existing solvers follow two distinct lines of work: trajectory-space methods, which refine sampling dynamics from random initial noise, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise itself. While most prior work treats these as independent design choices, we show that they are inherently coupled. We derive a unified stability bound that links initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity through a multiplicative envelope, complemented by two empirical observations. First, we identify a sufficiency regime in which a moderately optimized proximal source initialization is enough to attain the performance plateau, rendering exhaustive source-space optimization unnecessary. Second, this initial advantage is fragile: it is eroded by excessive stochasticity accumulation during guided sampling, necessitating a mechanism that bounds the cumulative noise injection. These findings motivate FLINT, a two-stage framework that operationalizes this coupling. FLINT establishes a high-fidelity starting point via a manifold-constrained proximal objective in only a few iterations, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule that helps prevent erasure of the initialization advantage. Across diverse inverse problems, FLINT delivers state of the art perceptual quality and competitive distortion metrics while maintaining superior computational efficiency.
items.title: FLINT: Coupling Proximal Initialization and Bounded Stochasticity for Flow-Matching Inverse Problems

items.summary: Audited research compendium supporting the evaluation of Big Five league representation as a candidate squad-composition performance indicator for FIFA World Cup knockout progression from 1998 to 2026. The release contains 1,584 first-knockout starting-eleven records nested within 144 team-tournaments across eight men’s World Cups and 48 national teams. The analytical framework evaluates three linked properties: discrimination between levels of format-harmonised knockout progression; incremental information beyond pre-tournament World Football Elo; and transportability of any increment to World Cup editions and national teams excluded from model estimation. The 1998–2010 historical extension preserves the frozen exposure, outcome and model definitions established for 2014–2026. Historical starter status derives from the Fjelstul World Cup Database and was cross-checked against RSSSF match details. Club affiliation and top-division status were adjudicated using tournament squad records and season-specific domestic-league reference files. The 2014–2026 subset retains the completed provenance audit, including 505 re-checked starter records, 13 starter-name corrections, 45 club-affiliation checks and seven Big Five reclassifications. Analyses include tournament-adjusted ordinal and cut-point models, AICc comparison with Akaike weights, 5,000 national-team cluster-bootstrap samples with bias-corrected and accelerated intervals, leave-one-edition-out validation, leave-one-national-team-out validation, a strict 2026 temporal and tournament-format holdout, and a predictive cluster bootstrap that refits both competing models within every fold and resample. Additional checks address collinearity, edition adjustment and dependence through within-edition permutation testing and an edition-level block bootstrap. Big Five representation was associated with deeper knockout progression before adjustment for Elo, but this association attenuated after adjustment. Model comparisons and held-out evaluations did not establish a stable, transportable increment beyond prior team strength. These findings concern the predictive information provided by current league representation; they do not distinguish the mechanisms through which players enter elite leagues or develop within them. Version 5.2.0 updates presentation and documentation only. Figure 1 presents the relationship between Big Five representation and Elo alongside the four primary ordinal-model estimates. Figure 2 displays the held-out difference in ignorance score between the joint Big Five + Elo model and Elo alone for each World Cup edition, together with the equal-edition mean and its 95% BCa interval. The former supplementary interval figure was removed; its underlying estimates remain available in the deposited machine-readable results. No data, frozen definition, model specification, inferential estimate, predictive score, random seed or substantive conclusion changed from v5.1.0. The estimand is knockout progression conditional on qualification for the knockout stage. These observational data do not identify a causal effect of Big Five employment, estimate the long-term developmental return to elite-league exposure or address group-stage qualification. The compendium includes analytical data, provenance records, analysis code, machine-readable results and publication-ready figures. The derivative dataset is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0, with attribution to the Fjelstul World Cup Database.

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. Model evaluation uses task-specific cross-validation strategies and selection criteria: F1-macro for classification and RMSE for regression. Supported models are optimized with Optuna when hyperparameter tuning is applicable. Evaluation results, optimization summaries, and provenance are preserved in task-specific artifacts. Selected models can be fitted on the full dataset, exported, and reused for prediction. The resulting evaluation evidence supports reproducible model comparison but does not establish external predictive generalizability.

items.summary: Existing generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement $\mathbf{y}_0$ is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, the image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint flow and show that they are governed by the conditional mean of the clean image given the current joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. items.summary: Repeated mobile GUI tests can reuse routes, locators, and recovery strategies from earlier executions. However, a route that worked in one workflow or app version may be irrelevant or misleading in another. We study how an LLM-based tester can retain useful experience while withholding entries contradicted by current observations. We present a maintenance contract for AdaptiTest in which reusable experience has an explicit applicability scope, trace provenance, and a lifecycle for confirmation, revalidation, and withdrawal. The contract reserves persistence for a Reflector role and treats recalled experience as advice. The archived implementation does not establish end-to-end enforcement of every specified mechanism. The design changes retrieved context, not model weights. The evaluation uses read-only Android workflows and archived internal comparisons. A six-task, three-repeat ready subset reports 18/18 completed runs with memory versus 3/18 without it, but a grounded single-agent control also solves the earlier hard-task slice. A separate cross-session probe is excluded from efficacy conclusions because of confounded route schedules and unvalidated state labels. We examine 13 selected real-update hazard records across nine subjects, distinguishing stale-locator observations from policy-based withholding and offline retrieval diagnostics. The latter do not measure live-device failures or actions saved. These events are UI changes, not confirmed regression bugs. The evidence supports a bounded design and case study; it does not establish general efficacy, superiority over independent GUI-agent systems, or unrestricted exploration.
items.title: Can LLM Agents Learn to Test? Maintaining Scoped Experience as Testing Evidence for Mobile GUI Testing

items.summary: MELITE is an open-source Python package for the evaluation and selection of supervised classification and regression models using numeric tabular datasets. It supports classification-only, regression-only, and mixed-task workflows. items.summary: Large language model (LLM) shopping assistants now recommend products in multi-turn conversations. However, reliable evaluation faces Data scarcity and Difficulty Standardizing Criteria. To address these obstacles, we introduce CARTBench for CART (Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines). For Data scarcity, we curate cases from real commercial shopping needs across 17 retail domains, pairing timestamped dialogue with 1,603 product records. For Difficulty Standardizing Criteria, we develop case-specific rubrics guided by Ideal Response Principles, distilled from excellent replies manually selected from successfully completed orders. These principles also guide Principle-Guided CART Prompting, our structured recommendation strategy. The experimental benchmark contains 1,328 expert-annotated criteria across Core, Excellence, and Safety. To answer the CART question, we evaluate 7 flagship commercial API models, including GPT-6.1-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, and 35B+ parameters open-weight models. In the first full-suite evaluation under the frozen rubrics, 3 of 10 models exceed 90% on Core, while none exceeds 45% on Excellence. Therefore, we identify an understanding-to-execution gap between required behavior and high-quality purchase advice. To examine these limitations, we diagnose shared failures in product evidence and unresolved needs, linked to changing requirements and decisive unknowns. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Da1yuqin/CARTBench.
items.title: CARTBench: Rubric-Based Evaluation of Shopping Advice for Complex and Ambiguous Requests with Timelines

items.summary: This record contains the code, a simulated benchmark dataset, and the result files for a study on detecting cyberattacks that are masked by AI data-center load transients in inverter-rich distribution grids. The manuscript itself is not included. Benchmark. The IEEE 33-bus distribution feeder is driven by 61 measured GPU power traces: 10 large-language-model training runs and 51 inference runs, recorded on A100, H100, H200 and L40S GPUs at 0.1 s. These traces form the load of an AI data center at bus 7, rated at 15–30% of feeder load. A photovoltaic inverter at bus 17 follows the IEEE 1547-2018 Category B volt-var curve. Nine channels are recorded at 10 Hz: three bus voltages, feeder-head P and Q, data-center P and Q, and inverter P and Q. The dataset holds 1,000 labeled scenarios of 120 s each. Of these, 598 contain one of seven attack types (bias, scaling, ramp, pulse, replay, coordinated mimic, and control-loop), and 220 of the attacks are hidden inside data-center load transients. Every sample is labeled for attack and for load transient. Code. The Python code covers: a linearized DistFlow model and an exact AC backward/forward-sweep power flow; data-center load generation from the GPU traces; attack injection and 10 Hz scenario simulation; physics-residual features learned from historical measurements, without feeder impedances; the RIME optimizer and a CNN-LSTM-attention detector (PR-Net); gradient-boosting, random-forest, MLP and logistic-regression baselines; window-level and event-level evaluation with scenario-bootstrap confidence intervals. Results. The result files contain the numbers behind all tables and figures: comparisons of detectors trained with and without load-transient awareness and physics residuals; ablations, computational cost, and an equal-budget comparison of RIME, random search and an untuned default; robustness tests under seven conditions, including exact AC power flow, unseen workload shapes, and changes in noise, photovoltaic share, data-center size and inverter location; a replay-attack consistency check; trained Stage-1 network weights. Third-party data. The GPU power traces come from the public LLM Power Trace Explorer repository (commit 9c25218). Because that repository has no license file, the raw traces are not redistributed here; scripts/prepare_gpu_traces.py rebuilds them from the public source. The included benchmark contains only simulated feeder signals driven by normalized, scaled versions of those load shapes.

items.summary: Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.

items.summary: This package reproduces all tables and figures of the article “Completing Ecosystem Knowledge Graphs: Few-Shot Learning with Calibrated Rules and the Governance of Innovative Start-ups”. The article builds LUCE-KG, an ontology-rich knowledge graph of 15,493 Italian innovative start-ups and SMEs and 25,982 persons. It proposes CRML, a few-shot learner whose predictions are explained by rules with empirical-Bayes calibrated confidences, and tests it on four graphs (FB15k-237, CoDEx-M, NELL-One and LUCE-KG). It then analyses 11,764 firm-years with panel estimators, clustering and explained machine-learning models. Contents code/ : the full pipeline, from graph construction through few-shot completion, baselines (MetaR, TransE, AnyBURL, LLM re-ranking), econometrics, clustering and machine learning, to the build of the manuscript; config/ : few-shot splits, fold assignments, selected hyperparameters and the LUCE-KG ontology; results/ : aggregated results from which every table is built; data_open/ : open-data extracts of the Italian register of innovative start-ups and SMEs (July 2026); README.md with the order of execution, and requirements.txt with software versions. Data not included. Officer and financial records from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) are licensed and contain personal data, so they are not redistributed. Licensed users can rebuild every input with the scripts provided. The public benchmarks are available from their original sources. Environment. CPU only (2 cores, 8 GB RAM), Python 3.13; the full pipeline takes about 40 CPU-hours. Funding. Project “LUtech Campus Ecosystem—LUCE” (Project Code 22ROJB5), Puglia Region, Program Agreement (Contratto di Programma).
